label: Title
notes: Open by framing triangulation as a translation device: it turns continuous geometric input into finite cells, edges, counts, and local moves. The lecture will keep returning to a single question: what certificate tells us this triangulation is the right one for the task?

label: Lecture Map
notes: Use this slide as the route map. Counting, flipping, empty circles, and special structures are not disconnected topics; each is a different kind of evidence about a triangulation. The audience should listen for which certificate is being invoked on each slide.

label: What Is Triangulated
notes: Pause on the distinction between polygon input and point-set input. A polygon gives the boundary first; a point set asks the hull to emerge from the data. Both become embedded planar graphs, but the bookkeeping variables have slightly different meanings.

label: Euler Ledger
notes: Derive the formulas verbally from Euler rather than presenting them as magic. Each bounded triangular face contributes three incidences, hull edges appear once in the boundary correction, and the outside face is what keeps the accounting honest.

label: Algorithms
notes: Emphasize that the computational object is not the plotted picture. The plot is a witness for humans, while the edge set, face list, and invariant checks are the reproducible mathematical output. Ask students where each possible bug would appear: a crossing violates geometry, a wrong face count violates Euler, and a missing hull edge violates coverage.

label: A Flip
notes: Describe a flip as the smallest possible edit that still changes a triangulation. This is the move that lets algorithms improve a mesh locally and lets the theory discuss connectivity among all triangulations. Point out that all four vertices of the quadrilateral remain fixed, so the operation changes incidence data without changing the input set.

label: Pentagon Flip Graph
notes: Use the pentagon as the smallest nontrivial state space. Students can see every triangulation at once, every edge in the graph is a flip, and the cycle foreshadows the associahedron without requiring a high-dimensional picture.

label: Why Delaunay
notes: This is the transition from counting all triangulations to choosing a useful one. The Delaunay criterion is introduced as a local geometric preference that tends to avoid poor angles and supports nearest-neighbor structure. Contrast the two drawings by asking which triangle would be more stable for interpolation, then connect that visual discomfort to a formal circle predicate.

label: Empty Circle
notes: Define the certificate in words before pointing at the formula. The circle is not decorative: it is the local predicate that a triangulation algorithm can check and repair with flips. Make the strict interior condition explicit, because points exactly on the circle indicate degeneracy and may allow more than one valid Delaunay triangulation.

label: Illegal Edge Flip
notes: Make the before-and-after interpretation explicit. A Delaunay algorithm does not need to rebuild the whole triangulation after every local failure; it can flip the offending diagonal and then recheck nearby certificates. The important teaching point is locality: only triangles adjacent to the changed edge need immediate attention after the repair.

label: Voronoi Shadow
notes: Do not prove the duality here; use it as orientation for why Delaunay structures matter beyond mesh aesthetics. The next chapter will make the Voronoi side primary. For now, highlight the reciprocal questions: Voronoi cells record nearest-site regions, while Delaunay edges record which sites become neighbors through shared cell boundaries.

label: MST Inclusion
notes: Stress the surprise: a global object computed from all pairwise distances is contained in a sparse geometric graph. This is a useful algorithmic theme, because Delaunay preprocessing can reduce the search space. Sketch the cut-property intuition: if an MST edge had an intervening closer point in the relevant lens, a shorter replacement would contradict minimality.

label: Pseudotriangles
notes: Use this slide to broaden the word triangulation. Pseudotriangulations keep a triangle-like combinatorial role while allowing faces whose boundaries are chains, which is useful in motion and rigidity contexts. Name the three convex corners and the reflex chains separately so students see why the object is not an ordinary triangle drawn badly.

label: Compatible Triangulations
notes: Explain compatibility as a promise that corresponding vertices and diagonals match. This is a useful counterweight to Delaunay: sometimes the desired property is not an empty circle, but preservation of a shared combinatorial skeleton. The two shapes can have very different coordinates, yet the same diagonal pattern lets one compare, morph, or interpolate them consistently.

label: 3D Warning
notes: This is a conceptual guardrail. Students often want the planar formula to have a simple spatial sibling, but tetrahedra introduce choices and degeneracies that Euler alone does not tame. Use the diagram to separate topology from geometry: Euler still exists, but it no longer determines the number or quality of tetrahedral cells from vertex and hull counts alone.

label: Worked Micro Lab
notes: Connect the slides to the computational notebook without making the lecture depend on opening it. The same certificates appear there as reproducibility witnesses: counts tables, flip graphs, circle overlays, Delaunay checks, and MST inclusion records.

label: Takeaways
notes: Close by asking students to name the certificate before naming the object. If they can say whether they are checking counts, flips, empty circles, compatibility, pointedness, or a dimension warning, they have the chapter’s logic.
